articles.title: Georgia, Azerbaijan Hold Intergovernmental Meeting, Talk ‘Speeding Up’ Border Process
articles.body:
Georgia and Azerbaijan signed documents, discussed cooperation, and agreed to speed up the border demarcation and delimitation process as officials from the two countries held the 11th meeting of the Georgia-Azerbaijan Intergovernmental Commission on Economic Cooperation on October 30 in Tbilisi.

The meeting, co-chaired by Georgian Dream Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze and visiting Azerbaijani Prime Minister Ali Asadov, focused on trade, energy cooperation, infrastructure, and Middle Corridor-related projects. Kobakhidze also told the journalists later that the two sides had agreed to accelerate the process of demarcating and delimiting their shared border, including the area around the historic David Gareji Monastery complex.

Following the meeting, Kobakhidze and Asadov signed the protocol of its 11th session, while the officials from the two countries also signed “an agreement on the practical operation of the joint Georgia-Azerbaijan international road border crossing point, Silk Road-Ipek Yolu, as well as memoranda of understanding on cooperation in the fields of veterinary services and plant protection,” according to the Georgian government’s press release.

Kobakhidze also held a separate meeting with Asadov, during which they discussed bilateral strategic partnership, cooperation across various sectors, as well as “the prospects for the Middle Corridor and the particularly important role of the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway in enhancing regional transport connectivity.”

According to the Georgian Dream government’s press service, officials from the two countries reviewed progress in trade and economic cooperation over recent years and discussed plans, with attention devoted to the Middle Corridor, “major infrastructure projects underway in Georgia, the successful partnership in the energy sector and opportunities for implementing new joint initiatives.”

The press service cited Kobakhidze as saying that “for centuries, our peoples have lived side by side, respecting each other’s traditions and national interests. It is precisely this mutual respect that has been and continues to be the solid foundation of our partnership.”

Kobakhidze noted that the two countries’ strategic partnership is reflected in their high-level political dialogue, pointing to Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Georgia in April, which, he said, “once again reaffirmed our mutual interest in further developing and deepening bilateral relations.”

He also addressed the “ongoing geopolitical developments in the region,” highlighting that Georgia has “always been a strong advocate of peaceful coexistence and dialogue in the region.”

Kobakhidze described Azerbaijan as “among Georgia’s largest trading partners,” saying the objective is to “build on the progress achieved, including by better utilizing the export potential of Georgian products, further diversifying trade relations and providing additional incentives for investment.”

He highlighted the Middle Corridor project, saying it’s “our shared objective” to “further increase the capacity, efficiency and competitiveness of this route.”

To achieve this goal, Kobakhidze said Georgia is implementing “large-scale infrastructure projects,” including the East-West Highway, the modernization and expansion of Georgian Railway, the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars (BTK) railway, the Anaklia Deep Sea Port and the new Tbilisi International Airport.

On energy cooperation, he highlighted the Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) oil pipeline, the Baku-Tbilisi-Erzurum gas pipeline, the Baku-Supsa oil pipeline and the Southern Gas Corridor, saying these projects “have for many years facilitated the reliable transit of energy resources while contributing to regional and European energy security.”

He also noted that, together with Azerbaijan, Romania and Hungary, “Georgia is participating in the development of the Green Energy Corridor, an initiative aimed at facilitating the transmission of renewable energy and strengthening the integration of the South Caucasus with the European energy market.”

Kobakhidze added that the agenda of bilateral relations “also encompasses defense, culture, education, agriculture, healthcare, tourism and customs cooperation,” saying Georgia stood ready to strengthen existing ties and facilitate new joint initiatives.

The press release also included remarks by Azerbaijani Prime Minister Ali Asadov, who noted that the strategic partnership had entered “a qualitatively new phase” in recent years, also highlighting Aliyev’s visit to Tbilisi and Kobakhidze’s visit to Baku in May.

He described Georgia as one of Azerbaijan’s “key trading partners,” noting that during “the first nine months of this year, bilateral trade volumes increased by over 40%, reaching 1 billion USD compared with the corresponding period of the previous year.”

“Our cooperation in the field of investment is also demonstrating very positive momentum. Azerbaijan has invested approximately 4 billion USD in Georgia,” he said.

On major infrastructure and energy projects, Asadov highlighted the Southern Gas Corridor, saying it plays a particularly important role in “ensuring energy security in the region and Europe.” He also noted that cooperation in the electricity sector is developing successfully and that the two countries are working on the Green Energy Corridor project to Europe.

He pointed to the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway and the increase in its capacity to five million tonnes, describing it as the “result of our successful joint efforts.”

Asadov also highlighted cultural and humanitarian cooperation, expressing hope that “construction of the new building of the Heydar Aliyev Tbilisi State Professional Azerbaijani Drama Theatre will begin in the near future.”

“The Azerbaijani and Georgian communities residing in our respective countries play a particularly important role in strengthening bilateral relations,” he was cited as saying. “Providing education in their native languages and the achievements of the relevant schools contribute to deepening the ties between our peoples.”

Speaking to the media following the meetings, Kobakhidze said the two sides “touched on the issue of border demarcation and delimitation,” including Davit Gareji Monastery and “the corresponding territory.”

According to Kobakhidze, the Georgian side “expressed hope that work on border demarcation and delimitation will continue at a very fast pace,” noting that “there has been no change over the past many years in terms of border demarcation and delimitation, and we need rapid progress.”

Kobakhidze added that they expressed that request to the Azerbaijani side, “to which we received a very friendly response,” and that “we agreed that we will speed up the processes related to border demarcation and delimitation.”

He noted that “there are approximately 15 such sections, and we need to work very actively on all fifteen. The main thing is to resolve the issue in principle, and for that, it is essential to complete the demarcation and delimitation process and to move forward in this direction, and that is exactly what we discussed today.”

This post is also available in: ქართული

articles.title: Man Arrested As Tourist From Belarus Alleges Attack Over Russian Speech in Tbilisi
articles.body:
The Interior Ministry confirmed that one person has been arrested, as Russian sources cited a tourist from Belarus alleging that a man physically attacked her at Tbilisi railway station because she was speaking Russian. The alleged assailant reportedly claimed that he hit her after she rejected his attempt to introduce himself.

The incident, which reportedly took place several days ago, was covered by Russian media outlets, including Lenta.ru, which cited reports from the Telegram channel Baza.

According to Baza, the woman, identified as Alexandra, a fitness trainer from Minsk, accused an unknown man of attacking her after hearing her speaking Russian with a friend at the railway station in Tbilisi. The woman subsequently contacted the police, Baza reported, adding that the man claimed in police custody that he hit her after she “rudely” rejected his attempt to introduce himself, an account the tourist denies.

The Interior Ministry confirmed the arrest to Civil.ge, saying he was arrested at the scene under Article 126 of Georgia’s Criminal Code, which covers beating or other violence causing physical pain and is punishable by a fine, community service, house arrest, or imprisonment for up to one year.

This post is also available in: ქართული

articles.title: International Reactions to Georgia’s Opposition Party Ban Proceedings
articles.body:
Georgia’s Constitutional Court has begun hearings in a lawsuit filed by 88 lawmakers from the ruling Georgian Dream-led majority seeking to ban five major opposition political groups. The lawsuit targets the United National Movement (UNM), Coalition for Change, Lelo/Strong Georgia, Federalists, and former Prime Minister Giorgi Gakharia’s For Georgia party.

In their lawsuit, Georgian Dream lawmakers accuse the opposition groups of pursuing unconstitutional objectives, undermining the legitimacy of elected authorities, and attempting to destabilize the country. The Constitutional Court accepted the case for substantive consideration in October, and hearings are ongoing, with the court having until June 2027 to rule on the case.

The proceedings have drawn international criticism, with critics warning that the proposed bans threaten democratic principles and political pluralism in Georgia.

Civil.ge has compiled some of the international reactions:

EU Parliament Adopts Resolution: The European Parliament adopted a resolution calling for the “immediate withdrawal” of the Georgian Dream’s constitutional lawsuit seeking to ban opposition parties, arguing that the proceedings amount to “eliminating legitimate political opposition” and are part of a broader strategy aimed at “turning Georgia into a one-party regime by eliminating political pluralism.” It says this follows the model of Russia and Belarus and “serves the Kremlin’s objective of keeping Georgia outside the European and Euro-Atlantic space.” Read in full here.

Joint Statement by MEPs McAllister, Ušakovs, and Juknevičienė: “We take note of Mr Kobakhidze’s call for a political dialogue with the European Union. Dialogue was never closed by Europe; it was emptied of meaning by Georgian Dream. In November 2024 the ruling party unilaterally suspended Georgia’s accession process, against its own Constitution and the will of its people. It then answered every recommendation from the EU institutions with new repressive laws, violence against peaceful protesters, and the imprisonment of opposition leaders and journalists. The European Parliament’s decision to limit formal contacts with the authorities was the consequence of these choices, not their cause. Our door has always remained open to the Georgian people, to civil society and to the democratic opposition. It will reopen to the authorities the day their actions, not their words, show a return to democracy, freedom and the European path. The timing of the proposal speaks for itself. It comes as the Constitutional Court opens hearings on Georgian Dream’s request to ban five opposition parties, including the last opposition party still represented in Parliament. A government that seeks to outlaw its political opponents cannot at the same time present itself as a credible partner for dialogue. This offer of political dialogue with the EU cannot be seen in any other way than a cover for dismantling political pluralism in Georgia […].”

Joint statement by the Council of Europe Congress co-Rapporteurs: “The Constitutional Court of Georgia’s examination of a request by members of the ruling party to ban five major opposition parties is deeply alarming. Such a ban could constitute a dangerous escalation and distance Georgia from its commitments under the European Charter of Local Self-Government and its Democracy at all levels of government cannot exist without political pluralism and effective checks on the concentration of powers. As we have already warned this year, the continued dismantlement of the foundations of Georgian democracy is a matter of grave concern. If the parties were banned, thousands of citizens could be prevented from participating in local democracy because of their political affiliation, as the Venice Commission recently alerted. Pluralism would de facto no longer exist in Georgian municipalities. We remain committed to supporting Georgia in fulfilling its obligations as a member State of the Council of Europe in safeguarding democracy, human rights and the rule of law at local level. We will follow the proceedings closely, as well as their implications for local democracy, to ensure that all Georgian citizens have a voice on matters closest to them.”

Alain Berset, Secretary General of the Council of Europe: “Georgia’s Constitutional Court is due to begin hearings on an application by 88 parliamentarians from the governing majority to ban five opposition parties. Without prejudging the outcome of these proceedings and with full respect for the principles of sovereignty and judicial independence, I call on the governing majority to uphold political pluralism and preserve the space for political opposition. Political pluralism is essential to a healthy democracy and central to Georgia’s commitments as a member of the Council of Europe. […] A governing party that seeks to remove democratic checks on its power weakens the very country it seeks to serve. These proceedings take place against a backdrop of growing restrictions on civil society, independent media and freedom of peaceful assembly. Taken together, these developments risk undermining the checks and balances essential to democratic governance in Georgia.”

Christian Wigand, European Commission Spokesperson: “The EU is closely following these lawsuits to ban five opposition parties, including, of course, the latest developments in Georgia’s constitutional court in relation to this case. These developments, alongside recent legal amendments and earlier statements about banning opposition parties, suggest a troubling instrumentalisation of the justice system. This risks undermining fundamental freedoms, democratic pluralism and fair political competition. So we’re following this very closely, and we will continue to follow this lawsuit […]. What I can say in general terms is that we have been very vocal regarding the Georgian Dream’s actions to suppress political opposition, journalists and activists. They unfortunately try to keep on or continue to limit the civic space. Georgian authorities must immediately release unjustly detained politicians, journalists and activists and reverse repressive legislation.”

Gudrun Kugler, OSCE PA Vice-President: “Stop the Attempt to Ban Opposition Parties and Return to the Path of Democracy. I am deeply concerned by the proceedings that just began before Georgia’s Constitutional Court, seeking to ban five opposition parties at the initiative of members of parliament from the ruling Georgian Dream party. Political competition must be decided at the ballot box and through open democratic debate, not by eliminating political rivals through legal proceedings initiated by the governing majority. Banning political parties is an exceptional measure that must meet the highest democratic and legal standards. These proceedings are particularly troubling amid serious concerns about judicial independence, including concerns raised by the European Parliament. […] In my capacity as Vice-President of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly, I call on the Georgian authorities to withdraw this lawsuit and to end politically motivated prosecutions. […] I also call for the release of opposition leaders and others who have been arbitrarily detained or imprisoned for political reasons, and for full respect for the right to a fair trial […]”

Niklas Wagner, Director for Eastern Europe, South Caucasus and Black Sea Cooperation of the German Foreign Office: “We are deeply concerned regarding the court proceedings to ban five opposition parties in Georgia. Political pluralism is essential to democracy & crucial for EU accession.”

ALDE Party: “The ruling Georgian Dream party is seeking to ban five opposition parties, including ALDE Party member Lelo, part of the Strong Georgia coalition. If successful, the move could leave hundreds of thousands of voters in political limbo. The country’s liberal forces are joining together to fight back. On 25 October, several ALDE member parties in Georgia joined a protest campaign in Tbilisi under the banner of the Opposition Alliance, with a clear message: “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better.” Lelo, which competed in Georgia’s disputed 2024 parliamentary elections as part of the Strong Georgia coalition, is now among the parties facing a ban. With the next parliamentary elections due in 2028, the move would sideline key political challengers and further restrict democratic competition. […] ALDE Party stands with Lelo and its liberal partners. As the Opposition Alliance takes its campaign to the streets, Georgia’s liberals are making clear that they will not accept a political system in which opposition can simply be banned. The fight for a free, democratic and European Georgia is far from over.”

Norwegian Helsinki Committee: “We condemn the Georgian Dream’s attempt to ban five opposition parties through the Constitutional Court. This comes amid a prolonged political crisis following the disputed 2024 parliamentary elections, widespread protests, repressive laws, restrictions on civil society and independent media and a growing number of political prisoners. […] Banning opposition voices will push the country further toward authoritarianism. The European countries and institutions must stand with the Georgian people and call for these efforts to be abandoned. Fundamental freedoms and Georgia’s international human rights commitments must be respected. Political opposition, civil society groups and independent voices must be free to operate without fear of intimidation.”

articles.title: Kobakhidze again says Tbilisi ‘ready’ to restore US-Georgia ties after chargé d’affaires meeting
articles.body:
Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze again said Tbilisi is ready to ‘restore’ ties with the US after meeting the newly appointed US Chargé d’Affaires Courtney Austrian on Thursday. The meeting comes amidst a now yearslong effective freeze in Georgia–US relations which began under the administration of former President Joe Biden and has continued into President Donald Trump’s term.

The US has had no ambassador to Georgia since the previous US ambassador, Robin Dunnigan, retired and left Georgia in July 2025. At the end of her term, Dunnigan said that Georgian Dream had sent a private letter to Trump that was ‘threatening, insulting, [and] unserious’.

She did not reveal the specifics of the letter.

During the meeting between Kobakhidze and Austrian, described by the US Embassy as ‘introductory’, the two parties discussed Georgia-US relations.

‘The Prime Minister once again confirmed that Georgia is ready to restore the strategic partnership with the USA from a clean sheet. Irakli Kobakhidze emphasised the important role of acting ambassador in this process’, the Georgian government said, regarding the meeting with Austrian, who was appointed in September 2026.

In August, Kobakhidze met the interim US chargé d’affaires Amy Diaz to discuss Georgia-US relations.

The meetings come amid a decline in US–Georgia relations. Washington suspended the US–Georgia Strategic Partnership mechanism in November 2024, after Georgian Dream announced it would suspend Georgia’s EU accession process until 2028.

The US State Department said at the time that Georgian Dream’s actions had violated the core principles of the strategic partnership, and condemned, what it called, the excessive use of force against protesters.

The US had already taken several measures against the Georgian government in the previous year including suspending more than $95 million in assistance to the government and imposing visa restrictions on individuals accused of undermining democracy.

In December 2024, the US Treasury Department sanctioned Georgian Dream founder and honorary chair Bidzina Ivanishvili under an executive order targeting Russia-related activities.

Georgian Dream leaders had repeatedly said that Trump’s return to the White House would lead to a change in US policy towards Georgia. However, the sanctions imposed by Washington were not lifted following his election.

In early August, the US decided to make its visa bond programme for Georgians permanent. The rules, introduced at the start of the year, oblige Georgians to post a bond of up to $20,000 to obtain a tourist or business visa Georgia is the only European country to be subject to the scheme and is also the only state in the region to be included in a list of ‘high-risk’ countries the US associates with overstays.

Aslan is a Georgian–Azerbaijani student expanding the age gap at OC Media as an intern. He enjoys working out 6–7 days a week and keeping up with Rustaveli Avenue’s renovation.

articles.title: Russian-Armenian sentenced to almost 10 years in Siberian prison over social media comments
articles.body:
Gevorg Grigoryan, a 23-year-old who holds both Armenian and Russian citizenship, has been sentenced to 9.5 years in prison by a court in the Siberian city of Chita over comments he had made on social media years before. Sources told the independent Russian media outlet Mediazona that Grigoryan had been angered by Russian inaction during Azerbaijan’s 2023 offensive into Nagorno-Karabakh, and wrote ‘Hitler should have destroyed them all’, referring to Russians, and that ‘after Ukraine, [Russian troops] will enter Armenia’.

Grigoryan was charged with spreading ‘fake’ information about the military, disseminating military ‘fakes’, ‘rehabilitating Nazism’, and calling for ‘terrorism’ and ‘extremism’. In a statement following his arrest in 2025, Russia’s Investigative Committee said he wrote ‘comments containing offensive language’ and also ‘openly supported the ideology of Nazism’.

The charges have become increasingly commonplace since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and accompanying crackdown on freedom of expression in Russia. There have been hundreds of documented cases over the following years of prison sentences being handed down for similar charges pertaining to social media comments or other statements criticising Russia or its military aggression against Ukraine.

While Russia was not treaty-bound to support Nagorno-Karabakh during the final offensive in 2023, it did have peacekeeping operations on the ground, which did not act to prevent the outbreak of violence. Under obligations of the Collective Security Treaty Organisation (CSTO), which both Russia and Armenia are members of, Russia was required to come to Armenia’s aid during Azerbaijani incursions into its internationally recognised territory in 2021 and 2022, but did not.

The failure of either Russia or the CSTO to act at that time has been a key factor in the turning of Armenian public opinion away from Russia, and has also led to Armenia freezing its participation in the CSTO.

Nate joined OC Media as an editor after a year at The Kyiv Independent, where he covered Ukraine, Russia, and the South Caucasus. He has a background in grant writing and reporting on post-Soviet geopolitics, with a focus on conflict-sensitive journalism and human rights.

articles.title: ‘I miss my Georgian friends’ — From South Ossetian fighter and lawmaker to advocate for peace
articles.body:
Timur Tskhurbati took up arms against Georgia more than once. Today, he believes there is no alternative to talking.

Every so often, Timur Tskhurbati visits the grave of a six-year-old girl, clearing it of overgrown grass and laying down flowers. When everything is in order, he sends photos to the girl’s father, Misha Tabatadze, whose parents and grandfather are also buried in the same cemetery.

Since the August 2008 War, there is one thing Tskhurbati has never been able to achieve: to bring Misha or his wife from Tbilisi to their daughter’s grave; the couple are ethnic Georgians from Avnevi (Auneu), a village in South Ossetia.

‘I asked our authorities to let him come for two hours’, Tskhurbati tells OC Media. ‘I could not make it happen’.

He says he even suggested that Tabatadze’s wife come without him: ‘Let his wife come. Because this was their first child’.

For Tskhurbati, the story is more than a personal tragedy; it is an example of what he sees as the absurdity of continued separation between Georgians and Ossetians.

‘Why not let them come? Let Misha’s wife sit at her daughter’s grave’, he says.

Tskhurbati, a South Ossetian civil activist, took up arms against Georgia during the 1990s conflict and also fought in the August 2008 War. He says he never liked military life or wearing a uniform, but felt that taking up arms was his duty, also volunteering to fight in Abkhazia.

Tskhurbati was also a member of South Ossetia’s first parliament who voted for independence. Yet today, he describes himself as one of the few people in South Ossetia willing to speak to Georgians about peace, though he notes: ‘It is not easy to speak, especially with Georgians who genuinely fought against me’.

But, he adds, he has many Georgian acquaintances with whom he has warm relationships.

‘We all want peace. We all know what death is, and we want an agreement’, Tskhurbati emphasises. ‘I am ready to do everything that depends on me to make sure that war does not happen again and that somehow we can reach an agreement’.

The conflict between Tbilisi and Tskhinvali (Tskhinval) began in the final years of the Soviet Union. In 1991, fighting broke out as South Ossetian forces sought separation from Georgia. A 1992 ceasefire ended the large-scale fighting but left most of South Ossetia outside Tbilisi’s control, with its political status unresolved.

For Tskhurbati, the conflict began even before the fighting of the early 1990s. He dates its beginning to 23 November 1989, when a convoy from Tbilisi headed towards Tskhinvali by bus and other means. Tskhurbati says he was among several dozen Ossetian men who stood in the road and joined hands to stop the convoy.

He recalls the moment as a turning point, saying it convinced those around him that they could no longer rely on others for their security and began pushing them towards arming themselves.

Tensions escalated again in 2008. The August 2008 War killed hundreds of people and displaced tens of thousands.

Tskhurbati believes that years of separation have only made reconciliation more difficult.

‘When people do not communicate, grievances accumulate’, he acknowledges.

Tskhurbati recalls growing up in Tskhinvali at a time when Georgians and Ossetians celebrated St Nicholas Day together.

‘I don’t remember any national hostility between us. There was no enmity. People would fight, of course, but not because they were Ossetians or Georgians. It was simply a fight between boys’, he says.

Tskhurbati says not everyone in South Ossetia approves of his contacts with Georgians.

‘People are different. Ossetians also don’t like that I talk to you. They ask me, “Why do you talk to Georgians?” But at some point, we have to talk to each other’, he insists.

He remembers coming to Tbilisi in the past and meeting Georgians who, he admits, changed his perception of the people on the other side of the conflict.

‘I came to Tbilisi, I met people, and I saw that there are normal people there who want relationships and peace’, he says.

He believes his own background could make his calls for dialogue more meaningful in South Ossetia.

‘I am not the only person in South Ossetia who fought. Everyone knows my name. When they see that a person who defended South Ossetia with a weapon is now in favour of negotiations, I think it has a positive effect’, he says.

Tskhurbati adds that he does not understand arguments that it is simply ‘too early’ to talk.

‘When people tell me, “It is too early”, I ask: who decides when it is too early?’

‘During the war, nobody told me, “Timur, don’t go, it is too early”. But now they are teaching me that it is too early to talk. The sooner we start talking, the better’, he says.

Tskhurbati knows that some people on both sides may find such conversations uncomfortable. But he argues that does not make them less necessary.

He speaks Georgian and can understand almost everything, he says. His own children, however, no longer speak the language.

‘I raised two sons. Both have families, but my sons do not speak Georgian at all. For them Georgia is a very distant country. For me, it is not far away. I want to sit down with Misha and have a drink. We used to do that often’, he says.

‘My generation will disappear, and that will be it. There will no longer be Georgian speakers among them. That is why it is better to reach an agreement’, he emphasises.

His friendship with Misha Tabatadze is one of the examples Tskhurbati returns to frequently, noting that they have remained close despite the conflict.

He recalls the two making an agreement: he would never come to Misha’s village with a weapon in his hands, and Misha would not come to his side either. But there was one exception; if their respective sides went to war, he told Misha, he would fight — and Misha should not take it personally.

‘Misha said I was right. That is why we kept our relationship’, he recalls.

During the fighting, Tskhurbati says he tried to save his friend’s house from being burned, but was ultimately unsuccessful. The house was looted and eventually destroyed. He did, however, make sure that two small children’s chairs from the house were brought to Tbilisi.

‘I said: “These chairs belong to his children; they have to remain whole and unharmed” ’, he recalls.

Tskhurbati also sent to Tbilisi the files he found in the burned-down house, along with a Bible and a videotape showing Misha’s deceased daughter.

Tskhurbati also recalls that Misha always kept good wine at home. He had a qvevri — a traditional Georgian wine vessel buried in the cellar — covered with a stone lid. As a keepsake from his friend, Tskhurbati made a stool out of the lid.

Today, Misha has six children, and Tskhurbati three. They joke about their respective grandchildren.

‘I have four grandchildren, and he has only two. I tell him, “Misha, you are still losing” ’, Tskhurbati jokes.

He also mentions another former opponent, Irakli Mujiri: ‘He fought against us, and I fought against him […] But it is easy for me to talk to him. We quickly find common ground’, Tskhurbati says. ‘I miss these people.’

For Tskhurbati, these relationships are evidence that former enemies can communicate without abandoning their own experiences or identities. Yet while he has warm memories of his Georgian friends, he cannot visit them in Georgia, stating that he was barred from entering the country around two or three years ago.

The last time he came to Tbilisi was for heart surgery in 2017.

‘Almost nine years have passed since then. I was given nine more years of life. I am grateful to the Georgian doctors’, he emphasises.

A friend of his also underwent bypass surgery in Gori.

‘Now we are not allowed to come. It is very strange’, he says.

Tskhurbati also believes that disputes over land should not prevent the two sides from discussing how people can live in the future.

As one example, he points to the Leningor district, known in Georgia as Akhalgori. Over the course of the Soviet and post-Soviet periods, this region saw its status and demographic composition distinctly change.

Tskhurbati offers his own interpretation of the district’s history and explains that, before 2008, he had been willing to consider an arrangement in which Georgia retained Leningor in exchange for Truso Valley.

He acknowledges that the situation has since changed and says the issue is now effectively closed.

For him, however, the broader principle remains.

‘We have to agree on the main thing: how we are going to live in the future’, he insists. ‘We can always agree on the details’.

He is also dismissive of arguments centred exclusively on territorial claims.

‘ “Our land, our land” ’ — forgive me, but I don’t take that seriously’, he says.

At the same time, however, he emphasises that South Ossetians ‘simply have nowhere else to live’, adding that he cannot imagine himself a refugee.

‘I will soon be 70. I cannot be a refugee. If I were a refugee, I would die from grief’.

‘We were forced to fight. We did not want war’, he says.

No matter the future, however, he rejects the idea that South Ossetia must look towards Russia. Indeed, for Tskhurbati, one of the biggest misunderstandings between Georgians and South Ossetians concerns their relationship with Russia.

‘When people say that we want to be in Russia — don’t believe that’, he says.

At the same time, he says South Ossetians do not simply want to return to Georgia. What he wants, he explains, is an agreement based on equal rights.

‘If you ask anyone in South Ossetia whether they want to remain in Russia, they will say yes’, Tskhurbati says, adding: ‘But they do not say it because they want to. They say it because they are afraid’.

The fear, he explains, is that without Russian protection, Georgia would attack South Ossetia. Even in the worst-case scenario, he argues, territory alone will not solve the problem.

‘Suppose Russia betrays us. There simply will not be anyone left in South Ossetia. Everyone will leave’, he believes.

‘If you really need the land, then take the land. And then what? There is plenty of land in Georgia itself that is covered with weeds. Land is not the main issue. In the 21st century, when people talk about land like this, it irritates me’, he says.

In any case, Tskhurbati says, ‘one good thing that came out of this war is that we understood what freedom is’.

‘People say we are Russian puppets. But whatever we are, we can make our own decisions’.

Tskhurbati also believes that language matters when it comes to how Georgians refer to South Ossetia. He says it is painful for Ossetians when Georgian politicians use terms such as ‘Tskhinvali region’ or ‘Samachablo’ instead of South Ossetia.

‘If they refused to call you by your name, wouldn’t you be angry? They don’t even address us by our name, and that is painful for us’, he says.

Tskhurbati spoke to OC Media from Tskhinvali — the nearest Georgian village, Nikozi, is only a few hundred metres away. He cannot see it directly from his window, but his sister lives a little further away.

‘From her balcony, you can see Georgia very clearly’, Tskhurbati says.

The line of separation is around 400 metres from where he is speaking with OC Media.

‘I hope one day we will reach an agreement’, he concludes.

For ease of reading, we choose not to use qualifiers such as ‘de facto’, ‘unrecognised’, or ‘partially recognised’ when discussing institutions or political positions within Abkhazia and South Ossetia. This does not imply a position on their status.

Lana Kokaia joined OC Media as a Georgia staff writer in August 2026. She has been a journalist since 2015.

articles.title: Pashinyan threatens to metaphorically ‘break arms and legs’ of election fraudsters
articles.body:
Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan has threatened to ‘break the arms and legs’ of people distributing electoral bribes, adding that he meant this ‘in the political sense of the word’. The remarks came as Pashinyan has started to introduce the idea that Armenia needs to establish a ‘state-centred’ opposition, expressing concern that his party’s vote share is so high in recent local elections that it might give the impression of ‘dictatorship’

Ahead of the June parliamentary elections, Armenian authorities arrested numerous opposition figures from across the main opposition blocs, with members of Strong Armenia particularly affected, on accusations of distributing electoral bribes. Authorities also published wiretapped recordings to support their claims. In turn, the opposition has rejected the accusations, describing the arrests as politically motivated pressure.

Pashinyan made the remarks during his weekly press briefing on Thursday, responding to a journalist’s question about what kind of opposition Armenia should have.

‘No electoral bribes should be distributed. We’re going to break the arms and legs of those distributing electoral bribes, am I making myself clear? — I mean that in the political sense of the word’, Pashinyan said.

Earlier this month Pashinyan voiced the need for a new opposition, after his Civil Contract party won nearly all local elections held in 21 communities in October.

Pashinyan said in a social media video he was ‘not happy that Civil Contract won 90% plus’ of the share of votes in some communities and outlined three remaining challenges.

‘Firstly, how can we ensure that the election results do not give the impression of dictatorship and authoritarianism? Second, how can we establish an objective public control mechanism in the communities where we have high levels of trust? Thirdly, how can we form a state-centred, young, intellectual, objective, and genuine opposition that is governed and directed only by their electorate and citizens?’, he said.

During Thursday’s briefing, Pashinyan also addressed what he described as a longstanding discourse in Armenia that had ‘resurfaced’ during the 2026 parliamentary elections. He said people spoke of certain individuals as being able to secure a specific number of votes for a party through vote-buying, administrative resources, and other means.

‘People talk about certain individuals, saying this person has 50 votes, this one has 100, this one has 200, and this one has 300 votes’, Pashinyan said, adding that every person in Armenia had only one vote.

‘Anyone who has more than one vote is my class enemy, and eliminating these people is my political commitment’, Pashinyan said, adding that he would ‘go after’ anyone claiming to control multiple votes, either through law enforcement agencies or political means.

Pashinyan went on to compare his proposed approach to a new revolution, contrasting it with the 2018 nationwide protests known as the Velvet Revolution of ‘love and solidarity’, which brought him to power.

‘Against this category, there will be a Great October Socialist Revolution, because we are going to smash them to pieces — in the political sense of the word. They must be uprooted. [...] Moreover, if it turns out that there are people with this kind of mindset within the Civil Contract, they are ten times more my class enemies’, Pashinyan said.

Pashinyan was referring to Russia’s October Revolution in 1917, which paved the way for Soviet rule.

A journalist since 2016, Arshaluys specialises in fact-checking and open-source investigations, with a focus on the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict, politics, and social and gender issues. She is also a strong advocate for media literacy and closely follows Armenia’s media landscape.

articles.title: Aliyev to skip Turkey-led summit for first time in more than a decade amid growing tension
articles.body:
Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev will skip the upcoming summit of the Organisation of Turkic States (OTS) in Turkey amid growing tensions between Baku and Ankara following a series of political disagreements. It is the first time in almost 15 years of the OTS that Aliyev will not attend an official summit.

Although Azerbaijani officials have attributed his absence to a busy schedule, the decision comes as relations between the two countries have come under increasing strain following a dispute over hijab restrictions in Azerbaijani schools, public criticism by Turkish officials, and a series of increasingly critical statements in pro-government media on both sides.

Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov will represent Azerbaijan at the summit. Other Azerbaijani representatives are also expected to attend events held on the sidelines of the meeting.

On Friday, Aliyev is expected to attend the awards ceremony for finalists of the FIFA U-15 World Cup and Festival in Baku. The tournament's final match and official closing ceremony are also scheduled for that day.

Foreign Minister Bayramov will lead the Azerbaijani delegation at the OTS summit.

Discord between the two allies emerged publicly after schoolgirls wearing hijabs were prevented from entering schools in Azerbaijan after new legislation was introduced.

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan’s chief adviser Oktay Saral and several ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) lawmakers criticised the restrictions.

Azerbaijan's ruling New Azerbaijan Party (YAP), meanwhile, described their statements as interference in the country’s internal affairs.

Saral left his position on 26 October with Turkish media reports having linked his departure to the discord between Baku and Ankara that his statements contributed to.

Another potential point of divergence between Baku and Ankara concerns the selection of the next UN Secretary-General.Azerbaijan's Foreign Ministry has welcomed the United Arab Emirates’ initiative to nominate Lana Nusseibeh for the position.

Turkey, meanwhile, has put forward former Foreign Minister Feridun Sinirlioğlu as its candidate.

Following confirmation that Aliyev would not travel to Turkey, several pro-government Azerbaijani media outlets published analyses discussing the reasons behind his absence.

An analysis published by the pro-government APA, titled Why did President Ilham Aliyev not travel to Turkey?, accused circles in Turkey of conducting an anti-Azerbaijani campaign and described Erdoğan's phone call to Aliyev as a belated gesture. The article also stressed that diplomacy was based on reciprocity.

The analysis recalled that Erdoğan had also skipped the informal OTS summit held in Shusha in 2024, where Turkey was represented by Vice-President Cevdet Yılmaz. Erdoğan attended the quarter-final match between Turkey and the Netherlands at the UEFA European Championship in Berlin on the same day.

Erdoğan also did not attend the seventh summit of the Conference on Interaction and Confidence Building Measures in Asia (CICA), held in Baku on 15 October this year. Turkey was represented by Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan.

Another pro-government outlet, Trend.az, published a similar analysis, attributing Aliyev’s absence to what it described as a campaign against Azerbaijan and its president in Turkey. The article also argued that such actions were more commonly expected from Iran than from Turkey.

Independent Azerbaijani journalists and media outlets operating outside the country have documented the increase in tension.

According to the outlet Open Azerbaijan, citing an unnamed source, Azerbaijani Parliament Speaker Sahiba Gafarova purportedly instructed MPs not to attend official events organised by the Turkish Embassy in Baku. The source also alleged that Gafarova had instructed MPs to reduce their contacts with Turkish officials.

Separately, journalist Ganimat Zahid, who lives in France, wrote on Facebook that Azerbaijani MPs with the ruling party YAP did not attend an official reception organised by the Turkish Embassy at Gulustan Palace in Baku to mark Turkey's Republic Day, as they were apparently prohibited from doing so.

He said that MPs belonging to other pro-government parties and those not affiliated with YAP were not subject to the same restrictions, which — according to him — explained their attendance.

Zahid also claimed that television channels had been instructed not to attend the reception or broadcast reports from the event.

According to his account, Azerbaijan was represented by the Minister of Digital Development and Transport, Rashad Nabiyev, who is not affiliated with any political party and left the venue shortly after delivering a speech.

The Azerbaijani authorities have not publicly confirmed these reported restrictions.

The dispute has also attracted attention in Turkey, where several media outlets have questioned Aliyev's decision not to attend the Ankara summit.

The Turkish newspaper Sözcü published an article asking why Aliyev had not travelled to Ankara despite Erdoğan personally calling and inviting him. Another Turkish outlet, Yeniçağ, questioned whether the dispute could be explained solely by the controversy surrounding hijab restrictions in Azerbaijani schools.

Meanwhile, the Azerbaijani outlet Time TV suggested that the disagreement stemmed from problems between the two countries' leaders. It also argued that Aliyev might have avoided the visit out of concern that he could face public protests in Turkey over the hijab restrictions.

Speaking at the summit on Friday, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan said there was no room for division in the family photo of Turkic states. He also said Turkey had assumed the OTS chairmanship from Azerbaijan and expressed his intention to advance cooperation within the organisation in several areas.

Erdoğan said the summit's theme had been set as ‘Turkey's Century: Unity in Language, Thought, and Action’.

Editor’s note: An earlier version of this article incorrectly said it was the first time that President Ilham Aliyev had skipped an OTS summit in its 17-year history. Aliyev did not attend the 2012 summit, which was instead attended by then-Prime Minister Artur Rasizade.

Rafiq Shahbazov is a journalist based in Tbilisi, covering political and social developments in Azerbaijan, as well as issues affecting ethnic Azerbaijanis in the region. He has worked with independent media outlets. His work focuses on human rights, environmental issues, and pressure on journalists and civil society.

articles.title: Tears Of Joy As Ukrainians Evacuated From Russian-Occupied Oleshky Reunite With Family
Food Lines, War Dead: The Way They Live Now In A Frigid Siberian Town
articles.body:
For a few days in mid-October, residents of Tura, a remote town in Siberia's vast taiga, might have been excused if they thought they were back in the U.S.S.R. One woman, in fact, said the situation was "worse than it was under the Soviets."

With temperatures hitting minus 15 Celsius, locals young and old stood in line for hours at a time outside the main food shop to buy a few bare necessities such as potatoes, cabbage, eggs, and milk and to fathom the precipitous prices they had to pay if they managed to reach the counter.

Efforts to establish a system allowing customers to head back to the relative warmth of their homes and return when their number came up --- a common tactic amid the frequent food shortages of the Soviet era -- fell flat.

"The vendors said, 'If you want to eat, you have to wait in line,'" said Svetlana, whose last name is being withheld for her safety. "There were no exceptions, even for children or the elderly."

"Then they started limiting quantities, no more than 1 kilogram per person. Literally something like a single potato for each family member, and every family member has to show up to get it," Svetlana said. "It's come to this: great Russia, rationing potatoes."

The shortages did not stem from Russia's invasion of Ukraine, although the nearly five-year full-scale war has taken a heavy toll on the town, claiming at least 34 men among its 4,000 residents and damaging its economy.

Instead, they resulted from a combination of formidable logistical challenges and poor planning -- a problem that is pervasive and sometimes deadly in Russia.

No road reaches Tura from Krasnoyarsk, the regional capital over 1,000 km to the southwest, and the town's lifeline is the Nizhnyaya Tuguska River. When low water levels made it unnavigable in July, authorities failed to establish an adequate alternative supply route, and shortages of many fresh foods hit this month.

Prosecutors have launched a criminal investigation against several officials on suspicion of negligence.

Some items such as fruit, meat, dairy products, flour, and bottled water all but disappeared, and prices more than tripled by official counts.

"Look at these prices: 1,100 to 1,300 rubles ($13-16) for a kilo of cucumbers," Svetlana said, adding that cucumbers had run out before her turn came. "1,800 ($22) for green onions, 1,000 for onions! Forget about peppers and tomatoes."

Olga, another local resident, said her mother had to come to the store because the staff wouldn't let her buy the elderly woman's share on her behalf.

Other families "brought little children with them. Otherwise, they wouldn't have given out rations for each person -- even though the saleswoman knows how many people are in the family," Olga said. "We didn't have such horrors even under the Soviets, my mother said. She remembers."

After a major crunch in mid-October, food is now being flown in by air and rationed, with limits on how much a single person or a family can buy.

But the most recent shipment was missing potatoes, onions, and cabbage after two flights were postponed due to weather. Food lines have persisted despite the resumption of air deliveries.

On October 21, the district administration reported that food supplies at several local schools would not last past the end of the month. Residents say the food that has been flown in has been bought up quickly, and they worry about getting through the winter. When the river freezes over, though, it can serve as a road.

"The shop assistants are trying to reassure us, saying there's still some grain left over, pasta, canned goods," Svetlana said. "What, are we going to feed the kids canned goods all winter?"

For some, the town's current predicament is a result of developments that have altered life in Tura over the years, both before and after Russia launched its war against Ukraine.

"Back then, we fed ourselves [by] hunting and fishing. And the supplies [brought in by the state] were plentiful," Olga said of the Soviet era. "Now there are no fish in the river, no reindeer."

Tura is at the heart of an area once populated mainly by Evenks, members of an ethnic group of traditionally nomadic reindeer herders who have lived in Siberia and other parts of North Asia for centuries. About 900 of Tura's 4,000 residents have Evenk roots.

The town was built on the site of an Evenk camp in 1927 and was the seat of the Evenk Autonomous District until President Vladimir Putin's government folded it into the Krasnoyarsk Krai in 2007, a downgrade at the hands of a state that activists say is suppressing the cultures of indigenous groups and other minorities.

Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the state has lured men to the front by offering substantial benefits and signing bonuses, incentives that are particularly attractive in economically struggling regions where jobs are scarce.

Among numerous reports with similar findings, a March 2025 report from the US-based Wilson Center think tank said men from Russia's indigenous communities "have been recruited at above-average rates and experienced higher-than-average combat death rates."

"About 20-25 of us [Evenks] have gone [to war] over the past four years," Tura resident Kachikan said. "Half have already died. Six have been buried, but there are some who have been missing for a long time, so it's unlikely they'll be found alive."

"Two members of the Udygir family have already [been killed], Timur and Romka. They're cousins, Oleg and Yury's sons. Dmitry, who's also related, hasn't been in touch in a while; there'll be a death notice about him soon, too," Kachikan said.

"He went on a contract. It's obvious why: to make money," he said. "There's no work here. The oil industry? They don't hire our people, only shift workers. You can't even get a job as a cook."

Another Evenk, Volodya Oyogir, "went missing in 2025, and there was a funeral this year; he was declared dead. His wife had been searching for him since the previous March," Kachikan said.

"Volodya was a good hunter from a prominent family," he said, pointing to his grandfather Nikolai Oyogir, a prominent Evenk poet and folklorist who died in 1988. "His poems were published in Soviet journals, he worked at a newspaper. And his grandson died in the war. Such is fate."

A database maintained by the Russian-language outlet Mediazona lists 34 war dead from Tura. It includes the Udygir cousins, who died at age 30 and 42, respectively, and Oyogir, who was 37 when he was declared dead.

"What kind of life is this? Folk crafts have been destroyed. Fishing has effectively ceased as a source of income," said Vladimir, a Tura resident.

"The Tunguska has been flooded with oil, so there are almost no fish left," Vladimir said, apparently referring to spills that polluted the river in 2023 and 2024.

"The nearest reindeer herds are beyond Surinda," a settlement some 400 kilometers away, he said. "There's no real government support, and the prices are exorbitant. That's why people go to this [war]."

Siberia.Realities is a regional news outlet of RFE/RL's Russian Service.

articles.title: Evacuation From Russian-Occupied Oleshky Completed, Kyiv And Moscow Say
articles.body:
Evacuation of residents from the Russian-occupied southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky had been completed as Moscow and Kyiv continued to stick to the temporary cease-fire brokered by US first lady Melania Trump.

Buses filled with civilians left the war-torn area for the first time in more than four years without incident, both parties have reported, with the localized cease-fire set to remain in effect until November 1.

No media source currently available

Russian ⁠human rights ombudswoman Yana Lantratova said in a social media post on October 30 that after arriving in Ukraine's Russia-occupied Crimea, one convoy of buses then headed toward Russia, while a second convoy was bound for Ukraine.

"We are concluding our humanitarian mission ⁠in Oleshky. ‌We are currently in the territory of Armyansk (in northern Crimea)," she said in a video posted on Telegram, adding that both sides had praised the high standard of its organization.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy later said those residents of Oleshky who wished to travel to Ukraine have crossed into the country on October 31, thanking the United States and Melania Trump for their mediation.

After reaching Anapa in southern Russia from Crimea, the civilians were flown to the Belarusian city of Homel and then transported by bus to Ukraine's northern Chernihiv region.

The circuitous route was needed to avoid roads along front lines that have been heavily mined and destroyed by the conflict, sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

"When the world pays attention, people are rescued. Further steps toward de-escalation and real progress toward peace are also needed," Zelenskyy wrote.

Before the evacuation, Oleshky residents had been trapped for months in the largely ruined city, which was cut off from the outside world, with little to no access to food, drinking water, medicine, or electricity.

"Until we got on the buses, we were still afraid," Oleshky evacuee Liubov told RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service on October 31. "We were so worried and nervous. Before that, we couldn't sleep at night, wondering how this would go."

As the evacuation from the war-torn city was unfolding on October 30, the Kremlin said the temporary cease-fire there should not be extrapolated to the broader peace settlement process in Ukraine.

Moscow has repeatedly said it was not seeking a partial easing of the conflict, urging a complete resolution that would include its demands, including full control over Ukrainian territories that Russian forces have been unable to seize on the battlefield.

Separately, Russia has intensified its airstrike campaign aimed at pressuring Kyiv into accepting its conditions for peace by attacking the country's energy and civilian infrastructure and leaving thousands without heat or electricity amid cold weather.

This year, however, the Ukrainian military has been increasingly responding to the attacks with campaigns of its own, targeting energy and military infrastructure inside Russia with long-range drone strikes.

On October 31, the Ukrainian military claimed that it had targeted the Russian state-owned Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defense enterprise in the Rostov region, using both drones and Neptune coastal missile systems.

It said that a “fire at a finished-products warehouse has been confirmed,” with damage reported to four production workshops, adding that the facility manufactures solid rocket propellant for ammunition used by multiple Russian missile systems.

The Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, is a strategically important industrial and logistics hub in southwestern Russia. Earlier in the month, Reuters reported that Russia had nearly finished building a major new base for launching jet-powered drones there in just six weeks.

Citing satellite imagery, the report said the site had been an empty field as of the end of August and had become a complex facility covering an area equivalent to around 126 soccer fields by mid-October.

Rostov has been under Ukrainian aerial attacks since September. The Ukrainian Security Service had earlier claimed to have targeted a number of “Russian aerial assets” in a special operation at a military airfield in the regional capital, Rostov-on-Don.

The US State Department has announced the approval of a critically needed sale of Patriot air defense interceptors to Ukraine worth $2.1 billion to strengthen Kyiv’s defenses against increasing Russian aerial attacks.

Zelenskyy, however, warned that the 500 missile interceptors could take “several years” to arrive.

Welcoming the US State Department’s move as a “strong decision,” Zelenskyy wrote in a social media post that “500 PAC-3 interceptors is a substantial number” and could form an effective defense package this winter, but noted that “deliveries may begin only in a few years.”

“We are asking our American partners to find a solution for the time when there is a real danger and a real need to use PAC-3 interceptors,” the Ukrainian president said while noting that that his country’s energy infrastructure is under Russian attacks.

The State Department said that the proposed sale of the missile interceptors, being purchased with funds from Canada, Germany, and Norway, will support the foreign policy and national-security objectives of the United States “by improving the security of a partner country that is a force for political and economic stability in Europe.”

The announcement of the proposed sale came after Zelenskyy repeated his calls on October 30, asking the United States to speed up the release of the interceptors, which are seen as the most effective weapon against the ballistic missile attacks from Russia.

In September, the European Commission approved 6.1 billion euros ($6.82 billion) in defense procurement for Ukraine.

This amount also included the purchase of US PAC-3 Patriot missile interceptors under special exception to EU rules. The European Commission did not specify how much money was allocated for these interceptors, citing operational security considerations.

At a closed-door meeting of the European Council in October, Zelenskyy told the participants how many Patriot interceptor missiles Ukraine would need to get through the winter.

Daud Khattak is a senior international correspondent covering the Near East in RFE/RL’s Central Newsroom. He was previously the managing editor of RFE/RL's Radio Mashaal.

RFE/RL's Ukrainian Service has seen its audience grow significantly since Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022 and is among the most cited media outlets in the country. Its bold, in-depth reporting from the front lines has won many accolades and awards. Its comprehensive coverage also includes award-winning reporting by the Donbas.Realities and Crimea.Realities projects and the Schemes investigative unit.

G20 Diplomats Meet In Atlanta Amid Divisions Over Russia, Ukraine
articles.body:
ATLANTA, Georgia -- Foreign ministers from the Group of 20 leading economies are gathering in Atlanta on October 30-31 for talks expected to highlight continuing divisions among Western governments over Russia's war in Ukraine, as the United States seeks to steer the forum toward economic growth, energy security, and trade.

The Atlanta meeting, chaired by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, comes ahead of a G20 leaders' summit scheduled for December in Miami, which US President Donald Trump will host. Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited, although it remains unclear whether he will attend.

The presence of Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Atlanta has revived a debate among Western governments over whether engaging with Russian officials at international gatherings risks signaling a return to business as usual while Moscow's war on Ukraine continues.

RFE/RL has learned that there will be no traditional family photograph ahead of the summit this year. While the reason for the change remains unclear, some Western diplomats are said to have been unwilling to appear alongside Lavrov in an official group portrait.

Western diplomats told reporters that organizers were considering holding two group photographs, one including Lavrov and another without him.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said he would not avoid a group photograph with all participants, as dialogue was part of his job. But he stressed there could be "no normalcy" with Moscow as long as the war continues.

"For the first several years after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the United States and its European allies were united in refusing to return to 'business as usual' with Moscow, including by avoiding legitimizing it through normal diplomatic engagement," Nicholas Lokker, an adjunct fellow with the Transatlantic Security Program at the Washington, D.C.-based Center for a New American Security, told RFE/RL.

"That consensus has since broken down," he added.

Tensions over engagement with Russia have surfaced at previous G20 summits.

At an August finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, European delegates made their displeasure known after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent held a bilateral meeting with Russian Finance Minister Anton Siluanov.

European representatives insisted Siluanov be excluded from the meeting's "family photo," Lokker said.

Ukraine's absence from the Atlanta gathering adds another point of friction. Washington limited invitations to formal G20 members, leaving Ukraine and South Africa off the guest list.

Moscow, for its part, has complained about the arrangements. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said visas for the delegation had been resolved only at the last minute, suggesting that "not everyone in Washington is happy" about Lavrov's participation.

Lavrov has said he intends to use the meeting to advocate reform of global economic institutions and a more multipolar world order.

The State Department says the United States wants to bring the G20 "back to basics" with an agenda focused on economic growth, deregulation, innovation, energy, and trade.

Other priorities include strengthening supply chains, protecting freedom of navigation, and improving access to critical minerals, food, and fertilizer. Washington is also supporting Poland's bid to become a full member of the G20.

The agenda reflects the Trump administration's emphasis on economic competitiveness and energy security and its desire to make the forum a venue for practical cooperation on issues affecting global markets.

James Lamond, a senior fellow with the Democratic Resilience Program at the Washington, D.C.-based Center for European Policy Analysis, said the focus on innovation, energy security, supply chains, and critical minerals was welcome.

But he told RFE/RL that discussions would likely be dominated by the wars in Ukraine and Iran, making it difficult for ministers to concentrate on the G20's economic priorities.

Lamond said Lavrov's presence would make a substantive discussion of Ukraine difficult, particularly because Kyiv is not represented at the meeting.

"Anything of substance cannot be negotiated without Ukraine being represented," he said.

He also pointed to growing European concerns about Russian hybrid warfare, citing an armed drone incident at Leipzig airport, sabotage at factories, damage to undersea cables, increased cyber intrusions, and false-flag hate crimes. Russia has denied involvement in such activities.

Those concerns, he said, underscore the need for governments to address security threats that extend beyond conventional military conflict, such as cybersecurity.

Energy security, another major US priority, will be difficult to address without considering the conflict involving Iran and the wider Middle East, he said.

US officials have told several countries in the region and other allies to prepare for the possibility of renewed US military strikes against Iran following the November 3 midterm elections, as well as potential Iranian retaliation.

The prospect of further escalation adds uncertainty to discussions about energy supplies and the security of key shipping routes, even if the conflict is not formally at the center of the Atlanta agenda.

Alex Raufoglu is RFE/RL's senior correspondent in Washington, D.C.

articles.title: Serbia after Vucic: The winners are losing patience
articles.body:
After the Student List's election victory, Aleksandar Vucic's power apparatus is disintegrating. People want justice as soon as possible. But the losers still hold sway in the judiciary and administration.

Aleksandar Vucic is accustomed to the spotlight. As Serbia's all-powerful president, loyal media outlets followed his every move for years. His TikTok outbursts led the evening news. But on October 25 he lost the election to the Student List, and since then, a lot has changed.

Vucic complained at a press conference, before fewer microphones than usual, that the winners were practising "revolutionary terror." He threatened: "If they continue to terrorize those who think differently – beatings, destruction and all the rest – and the state authorities do nothing, we will be forced to organize ourselves."

Vucic regards the immediate resignation of the general director of the Serbian state broadcaster RTS as an example of this "terror." Senior RTS editors have also been dismissed.

On Monday, a small group of protesters invaded the Informer TV station. Thousands of complaints have been lodged against Informer over the years for its demonization of Vucic critics. Now, journalists' associations are calling for its license to be revoked.

Tabloid media outlets loyal to Vucic have already changed their tone. Unlike Informer, they no longer refer to the Student List as "terrorists" and "mercenaries."

The List, which emerged from the student revolt, is made up of professors, activists and artists. In the election on October 25, it won 53% of the vote, leaving Vucic's Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) trailing with just 39%.

Since then, things have moved fast. In many cities, citizens peacefully removed portraits of Vucic from municipal buildings. The public prosecutor's office for organized crime has launched investigations, including into electoral fraud. A special commission is examining the work of the Higher Public Prosecutor's Office in Belgrade, which critics say did Vucic's bidding, and persecuted his opponents.

The accusations against him are old ones: that he and his system kept the media under tight control; that state contracts were only awarded to companies loyal to the regime; and that Vucic, his party, and the Serbian state had links to organized crime.

The catalyst for the revolt was the collapse, two years ago, of the concrete canopy on the newly renovated railway station in Novi Sad. Sixteen people died. The accident is believed to have happened as a result of poor workmanship and corruption in the awarding and execution of the renovation contract.

Those who were celebrating in the streets a few days ago are already growing impatient. The new parliament has not yet been convened, and the SNS still controls many levers of power.

"A society that was oppressed for so long by a party that acted like a feudal lord now, understandably, expects justice," Dejan Bursac from the Institute for Philosophy and Social Theory at Belgrade University told DW. "In this power vacuum, people are getting impatient."

Vucic and leading officials promise to be a strong opposition, and expect to make a quick comeback once "this lot" have ruined the country. But the majority of critics are calling for Vucic to be investigated and charged. "The SNS people are acting as if they had lost a local election somewhere in democratic Scandinavia, not as if they were part of a deeply corrupt and criminal regime," said Bursac.

It's very common in Serbia for politicians to switch allegiance from one camp to another. They go where the power is. Even Vucic has admitted that many of his former comrades-in-arms are turning their backs on him. "We are going to see cases of people resigning or staying in the shadows, even putting themselves forward as informants for the next government," said Zlatko Minic from Transparency Serbia, an organization that monitors the work of governments.

The million-dollar question is: How much damage can the old government do to the new one? "There's still time for many officials to award contracts and create financial obligations for the agencies they run without necessarily committing a criminal offense," Minic warned.

However, those familiar with the situation said that for some time now the Student List has had contacts with officials in the police and administration opposed to Vucic's style of government. The winners of the election may now be able to prevent certain actions. On Wednesday, the List again demanded the resignations of leading officials in the police and judiciary. Whistleblowers were also asked to come forward if the outgoing government should try to "destroy documents."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a symbolic move, Student List representatives held their first press conference in Pioneers Park in front of the parliament building. Vucic's followers fenced off the park in 2025, turning it into a pro-government encampment. According to investigative journalists, it also became a base for thugs and criminals who attacked anti-government demonstrators. The morning after the Student List's election win, its supporters went out with binbags and cleaned up the park.

The victorious Student List unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focussed on making changes in domestic politics, and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

"Our plan is to stabilize and develop the country, not to destabilize it with some abrupt change of course on foreign policy," Oliver Toskovic, a psychology professor and future member of parliament, told DW.

Toskovic said that, unlike under Vucic, the EU will not be misused as a "cover." Serbia's EU accession process recently stalled, with Vucic accusing "the West" of inciting a "color revolution" in Serbia.

"We are very dependent on Russia for energy. This is really a mistake of the previous government," Toskovic said. "But for that reason, sanctions right now would destabilize the country. And that would not be good for us or for the EU." How energy policy will develop under a Student List government is still unclear.

Where Vucic would frequently take aim at Kosovo, Croatia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading representatives of the new List have promised better relationships with Serbia's neighbors and a reduction in tensions. On Kosovo, Ilija Srdanovic, the Student List's lead candidate, has said the party is open to dialog with the government in the Kosovar capital, Pristina. He has already spoken by phone with the prime minister of Croatia.

The electoral process is not yet over. On Sunday, November 1, the vote will be repeated in some 50 polling stations because there were irregularities first time around. Once these votes are counted, parliament can be convened. The formation of a government is expected to be quick, but for now the names of the prospective members have not been disclosed.

This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: More than 290 arrested in France as some weekend protests turn violent
articles.body:
Protests continue across France as 320,000 people take to the streets over rising living costs and poor school conditions for a third consecutive weekend, with clashes reported in several cities.

A number of clashes have been reported between protesters and police in several French cities on Saturday as hundreds of thousands of people again took to the streets nationwide to protest the rising cost of living and conditions in schools.

The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people had participated in demonstrations across the country, including 70,000 in Paris.

"The marches proceeded smoothly within the framework of the declared demonstrations," the ministry said, while noting that "radical elements" in several cities, including Bordeaux, Toulouse and Marseille, had attempted to enter city centres "with the aim of carrying out vandalism and looting."

In Marseille, footage showed fires burning in the streets as firefighters responded. Clashes with police were also reported in Rennes and Toulouse.

After a largely peaceful start to the day, police fired tear gas in Paris and Lyon in the late afternoon, according to French media reports and live broadcast footage. Tensions in the capital escalated as demonstrators reached the end of their march on the city's southern outskirts.

Footage aired by BFMTV showed fireworks exploding and incendiary devices being thrown at officers in riot gear, with several officers caught in the flames.

Paris police carried out more than 1,200 checks at railway stations and nearby areas early on Saturday to identify potential troublemakers, the city's police prefecture said.

The checks aimed to prevent demonstrators from bringing fireworks, knives and other prohibited items to the marches.

Police also deployed "all available resources" in the air to monitor security throughout the day, the prefecture said. An official order authorized camera-equipped drones to capture and transmit live images of the situation across the capital.

More than 290 arrests were made on Saturday across France, according to police.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez warned earlier Saturday that the demonstrations posed a "very high risk," citing calls for looting and rioting.

Around 70,000 police officers and other security personnel were deployedacross the country to maintain order during the protests.

Authorities also feared that Halloween celebrations could give people an opportunity to conceal their identities while committing offenses.

Amid concerns over attacks on public buildings and looting, officials ordered protest routes in Paris and other cities to be moved away from city centers.

Many shops and businesses responded by boarding up their windows and taking other precautions. Curfews and other restrictions were also imposed in several cities, including measures targeting specific areas and minors.

A similarly large security deployment last weekend largely prevented a repeat of the violence and destruction seen during the October 17 protests.

Young people have been taking to the streets for weeks to protest inadequate staffing and equipment in schools. Since mid-October, other groups have joined the demonstrations, mainly over the rising cost of living.

Trade unions, school and student organizations, and the grassroots Yellow Vest movement, which first rose to prominence in France in 2018, called for Saturday's protests.
