articles.title: Israel's election results are in. Here's what could happen next
articles.body:
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Israeli election results are in, showing the makeup of the country's next parliament but leaving open the question of who will be prime minister.

Party leaders will now hold high-stakes negotiations as they try to cobble together a 61-seat coalition in the 120-member assembly, known as the Knesset.

WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock

It's a tough path ahead for both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot. Neither of their camps won a majority, and Arab-led parties, which won a historic 19 seats, could play a decisive role.

Any possible coalition would require candidates to make tough compromises that could outrage their own voters. If they are unable to do so, new elections would be held early next year, with Netanyahu's government staying on as caretaker until then.

Here is a look at the possible scenarios:

On paper, the most straightforward solution would be for Eisenkot to join forces with the Arab-led parties in a solid, 67-seat coalition opposed to Netanyahu. Even if they don't join his coalition, they could provide crucial backing for a minority government.

But that would be politically risky for Eisenkot and his Jewish allies.

Israel's Arab citizens, who make up 20% of its population, are Palestinians whose families remained in Israel after the 1948 war surrounding its creation. They have close ties to Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and largely support their cause, leading many Jewish Israelis to view them with suspicion.

Only once has an Arab party joined a governing coalition, in 2021, and that government only lasted around 18 months.

Netanyahu is already portraying any such alliance as a betrayal of Israel's Jewish identity and a national security threat, raising the pressure on Eisenkot's allies, particularly those on the right, to reject it.

Netanyahu could try to convince Eisenkot and his right-leaning allies to instead ally with the prime minister.

This constellation could give Netanyahu a 67-seat majority and would send Arab-led parties, as well as ultranationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish factions, to the opposition. Such a government could tackle pressing issues like military exemptions for the ultra-Orthodox or work to shore up Israel's economy.

It would require a lot of promise-breaking, though.

WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us

Eisenkot and his allies have vowed not to sit in government with Netanyahu after blaming him for the security failures surrounding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023 attack, accusing him of undermining Israel's democratic institutions and highlighting his ongoing corruption trial.

A government led by Netanyahu is unlikely to approve an official inquiry into the Oct. 7 attack, a central demand of opposition voters. And in the past, when Israeli opposition leaders have defied their voters to join Netanyahu, their political support has plummeted.

The arrangement would also require Netanyahu to jettison far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies who stood by him after the attack and through multiple wars and other crises.

Netanyahu is likely looking for weak links in the opposition bloc, which spans Israel's political spectrum.

He could try to lure some of his former allies, like right-wing party leaders Naftali Bennett or Avigdor Lieberman. Both strongly support nationalist policies like expanding settlements in the occupied West Bank, and would find it particularly difficult to partner with Arab parties.

WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election

But they have clashed with Netanyahu, often on personal terms, for years, and had vowed not to partner with him. They are also deeply opposed to the military exemptions that are a make-or-break demand of Netanyahu's ultra-Orthodox allies.

Eisenkot has fewer possibilities, as Netanyahu's right-wing Likud, and his far-right and ultra-Orthodox allies, have been fiercely loyal to him over the years.

If neither side manages to secure a majority, the country could be headed toward another election, likely early next year. Netanyahu's government would remain in a caretaker role until then.

This scenario could be disastrous for Netanyahu's opponents, who had momentum heading into this election, even though the outcome fell short of their expectations. They enjoyed a boost from tens of thousands of Israelis who flew in from abroad to vote but might not travel a second time.

Netanyahu would meanwhile buy time to shore up his coalition. Smaller right-wing parties that failed to meet the threshold for entering parliament essentially wasted pro-Netanyahu votes. They might not run a second time, or their supporters might switch over to the bigger far-right parties, strengthening the prime minister.

After a similar stalemate in 2019, Israel held five elections in 3 1/2 years.

Tia Goldenberg has been covering Israeli politics for nearly two decades.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: A historic vote born of fear and frustration for Palestinian citizens of Israel
articles.body:
SAKHNIN, Israel (AP) — For Palestinian citizens of Israel, it was a rare moment of political triumph.

Hundreds of thousands voted in record numbers, giving two Arab-led parties their largest-ever number of seats in Israel's parliament.

Many boycotted past elections, seeing little point. But after years of their communities being demonized or neglected, some of Israel's most marginalized citizens turned to the ballot box to fight back against the most right-wing government in the country's history.

"We are here and we're not on the sidelines," declared Mansour Abbas, leader of the Ra'am party, as supporters cheered in a wedding hall Tuesday night, watching the exit polls.

WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock

The surge makes them a major political force that could enable opposition parties to assemble a coalition to oust Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

But the question is whether Netanyahu's main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, and other opponents will ally with them. Only once has an Arab-led party ever served in an Israeli government. During the campaign, Netanyahu had accused his main opponents of planning to form a coalition with them, which Eisenkot denied.

Netanyahu and his allies are now turning up the anti-Arab rhetoric even further, making unproven claims that foreign powers bribed voters to back Arab-led parties. In a Thursday post on X, Netanyahu warned against any party forming a government with them, saying it would lead to the "Islamization of Israel."

Nearly 840,000 people on Tuesday voted for Ra'am and the Joint List, a coalition of three Arab-led parties, a 64% increase from the last elections in 2022, according to final results from the Central Election Committee.

The parties won 19 seats in Israel's 120-member Knesset, surpassing the previous record of 15.

Crowds packed polling places in Arab communities from the Negev Desert to the northern Galilee.

In Tarabin, a Bedouin village in the Negev, Netanyahu's party had won majorities the past two elections. Turnout nearly doubled on Tuesday and Ra'am won 93% of the vote.

WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us

The northern town of Sakhnin had Israel's highest voter turnout, at 87%. Mayor Mazen Ghnaim said voters saw it as an emergency measure to fight rising violent crime in Arab communities and incitement by Netanyahu's far-right allies.

"I want to protect my constituents from being killed, my children from being attacked at their universities and Arab doctors getting attacked at hospitals," said Ghnaim, a Ra'am supporter, referring to recent incidents of anti-Arab violence.

The parties worked hard to overcome past reluctance to vote among Palestinians, who have long felt ignored in the halls of power. They held community meetings in cities and towns that Jewish-led parties mostly ignored. A grassroots movement went door-to-door in Bedouin villages to encourage women to vote.

Voters and candidates said their heightened participation did not reflect faith in Israeli democracy — it was a sign of desperation to unseat Netanyahu.

Two of his far-right allies, Itamar Ben Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, are responsible for some of Israel's most extreme policies and anti-Arab incitement.

WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election

Ben Gvir, the national security minister, raised alarm on Election Day over Arab turnout, telling his supporters, "If you want this country to remain Jewish and Zionist … then get out and vote!"

The rhetoric, also echoed by Netanyahu and Smotrich, may have only galvanized Arab voters.

"We see the government going from bad to worse," 52-year-old Awni Zoabi said after voting in Nazareth. "We want to live, we want a future for our children, and we want a future for ourselves."

Palestinians who managed to stay in Israel after the 1948 war surrounding its creation — when hundreds of thousands were expelled or fled — today, along with their descendants, make up more than 20% of the population. They have Israeli citizenship, including the right to vote, but also feel deep solidarity with Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank.

Ra'am and the Joint List both campaigned on combating crime and securing investment for Arab communities. But they offered different visions for how to approach the wider conflict.

Ra'am made the advantages of joining a coalition government central to its pitch to voters and said little that could alienate potential Jewish allies. It placed a Jewish former police official second on its candidate list.

In contrast, members of the Joint List called Israel's campaign in Gaza a genocide and compared the occupation of the West Bank to apartheid South Africa. Most Jewish Israelis ardently reject both accusations.

"People are clever enough to see what's happening. Of the two options, one is proposing a genocide, and the other is proposing apartheid. These are the choices: bad or worse," said Sami Abou Shehadeh, the leader of one of the slate's parties.

Mainstream Israeli parties have long resisted partnering with Arab-led parties elected to the Knesset, portraying them as threats to Israel's Jewish character or questioning their loyalty to the state.

Netanyahu's opponents welcomed Ra'am into a short-lived coalition government in 2021, in return offering investment in Arab communities and legal status for unrecognized Bedouin villages facing the threat of demolition.

The Islamist party's inclusion broke a longstanding taboo and gave it newfound political influence.

But given Israel's rightward shift, it will be difficult for Eisenkot to maintain support if he partners with Arab-led parties this time, said Tamar Hermann, senior research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute.

Israel, she said, has been "moving away from a liberal democracy and moving toward an ethnic democracy where one ethnicity has advantages over others."

Ra'am and the Joint List could handily give Eisenkot the numbers needed to form a government. Both have expressed openness to anything that removes Netanyahu, including abstaining from a Knesset leadership vote to lower the threshold Eisenkot would need to win a majority.

But in public, rather than court them, Eisenkot has set conditions, including that they profess that Israel is a Jewish and democratic state and declare Hamas a terrorist organization "to be demolished."

Leaders of both parties have condemned Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack on Israel but have balked at labeling the group a terrorist organization, in part because it would appear to justify Israel's devastating campaign in Gaza. Abbas acknowledged Israel as a Jewish state in 2021, while some Joint List leaders have questioned whether a country can be both democratic and privilege members of one religion.

Abbas said Tuesday that he was confident Ra'am would join a government. But his party did not respond to questions this week about whether it would accept Eisenkot's conditions or what its own terms were.

Yousef Jabareen, the Joint List's leader, told The Associated Press on Wednesday he had not yet spoken to Eisenkot but was ready for talks. He said parties on his slate had not agreed on their conditions, but hoped for protections and equality for Palestinian citizens, and promises to revive the peace process.

Above all, he recognized the desire to see Netanyahu gone.

"We have promised our community to do our best to get rid of this fascist government," Jabareen said.

Associated Press writer Tia Goldenberg in Tel Aviv, Israel, contributed to this report.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Difficult negotiations lie ahead in Israel after Netanyahu's bloc lost its parliamentary majority
articles.body:
JERUSALEM (AP) — Israel's final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his allies lost their parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.

The results released early Friday showed Netanyahu's bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday's election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-member Knesset.

Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.

"Now comes the truly hard part," centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: "If you want to know if something's happening behind the silence you're hearing now, the answer is yes."

Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?

Israel largely shuts down on Friday for the Jewish Sabbath, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Jewish-led parties to embrace them.

WATCH: What's next for Israel after election produces political gridlock

"There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties," said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.

The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes — Netanyahu — or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.

If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.

In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had "stolen" the election, potentially with foreign assistance.

The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing Arab citizens, who make up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over his far-right government.

On Friday, Netanyahu again warned against forming a coalition with Arab parties.

The head of Israel's election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said "serious suspicions" of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.

Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahu's party accused Qatar of involvement, allegations the Gulf state dismissed as "ridiculous and dangerous." Many Israelis view Qatar as a patron of Hamas, while Qatar says its relations with the militant group are part of its U.S.-backed mediation efforts in the region.

The election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been "entirely unfounded."

"It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population," he said.

WATCH: Projections show no clear winner in Israel's election

By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.

The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to "cast aspersions" on an entire section of the population that "exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner."

The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that "allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless."

The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkot's bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.

Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021.

WATCH: Retired Israeli general on what the election results tell us

"I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel," said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa.

Issa Jaber Abu-Ghosh, the former mayor of an Arab village outside Jerusalem, said "Israel all the time claims to be the only democracy in the Middle East," but that it's not a "real democracy" if its politics remain divided between Jews and Arabs.

If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be politically weakened as he faces an ongoing corruption trial, and an official inquiry into the security failures surrounding Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack would almost certainly be launched.

Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue.

articles.title: Aid operation and evacuations in Oleshky amid brief truce agreed to by Russia and Ukraine
articles.body:
KHERSON, Ukraine (AP) — A humanitarian mission entered the devastated city of Oleshky on Friday, officials said, as Russia and Ukraine observed the most significant truce of the 4½-year war that began with Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor.

A convoy including 25 buses, ambulances and aid supplies was due to arrive in the Russian-occupied city to deliver food and medicine and evacuate residents wishing to leave for Russia or Ukraine. About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, according to authorities and volunteers.

A localized ceasefire in Ukraine's southern Kherson region has held for four days and is due to continue through Sunday evening to allow the operation to proceed.

WATCH: News Wrap: Ceasefire in Oleshky holds for a third day

"Everyone who wishes to leave Oleshky will have the opportunity to do so safely," Russia and Ukraine said in identical statements. "Those who choose to stay may remain and will receive all the humanitarian support they need."

Officials from both countries worked together in a rare joint humanitarian effort, offering a brief bright spot in a grim war of attrition.

The United States played a central role in the mission, which the White House said was brokered by first lady Melania Trump. Pope Leo XIV also pressed Russian and Ukrainian leaders to help Oleshky.

Fighting continued elsewhere, however. Russia's Defense Ministry said air defenses downed more than 1,000 Ukrainian drones overnight, while Ukraine's air force said Russia launched ballistic and other missiles, along with scores of drones.

The convoy assembled in Armiansk, a town in Russian-occupied Ukraine about 85 kilometers (53 miles) south of Oleshky, said Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine's ombudsman and chief negotiator.

Demining of designated routes into the city was completed late Thursday, officials said. Two people were killed during the work.

Video posted by Lubinets' office showed him meeting older residents in Oleshky. One woman tearfully hugged him as others smiled.

Lubinets said evacuations would continue until 2 p.m. local time, with aid distribution beginning 30 minutes later. It was unclear whether he meant Ukrainian time or western Russian time, which is an hour ahead.

Ksenia Arkhipova, a volunteer who previously lived in Oleshky and remains in contact with residents, said large numbers of Russian military personnel were in the city.

"They are currently checking empty houses, and in some cases, moving into them," she told The Associated Press. "They are also pressuring local residents to evacuate to Russia, rather than to Ukraine."

WATCH: U.S. must put pressure on Russia so Putin ends the war, Ukrainian official says

Arkhipova said Thursday that about 1,000 residents had told her they wanted to leave. She said the Ukrainian delegation's presence was important because many residents feared Russian authorities would interrogate or detain them.

The evacuation route was not disclosed. Ukrainian-held territory lies just a few kilometers (miles) across the Dnipro River from Oleshky.

But Ukrainian public television reported that those heading to Ukraine would travel hundreds of kilometers (miles), entering the country through its northern border with Belarus.

Authorities have invited a small number of Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. media organizations to cover the operation in Oleshky.

Associated Press writers Susie Blann and Derek Gatopoulos in Kyiv, Ukraine and Yuras Karmanau in Tallinn, Estonia contributed to this report.

Oleshky evacuation begins as former U.S. Ambassador to Ukraine calls Vladimir Putin an “obstacle” to talks
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A large evacuation and humanitarian mission is currently under way in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Oleshky on the Dnipro River. The temporary ceasefire that made the truce evacuation possible, brokered by U.S. First Lady Melania Trump, is a rare example of successful Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Speaking to VOA, a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine says this temporary ceasefire is proof progress towards peace can be made.

On Friday morning, a delegation of Russian and Ukrainian human rights officials entered the war-ravaged town, and residents began boarding a convoy of buses to leave.

The convoy of about 25 buses arrived in Oleshky via Russian-occupied Crimea, about 85 km away. Ukraine’s ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said the road had to be demined before the buses could travel safely. Two people were killed during the demining according to Russia’s human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova.

Residents of Oleshky can choose to go to Ukraine or Russia. Residents who choose to go to Ukraine will travel to Russia, then fly to Belarus before crossing into Ukraine. Others are choosing to stay in Russia. About 2 thousand people were living in Oleshky when the evacuation was announced. Over 500 evacuees are choosing to relocate to Ukraine.

William B. Taylor, an expert at the Atlantic Council who served as U.S. Ambassador (2006-2009) and later as Chargé d’Affaires (2019–2020) in Ukraine, spoke to the VOA Russian Service about the prospects for the temporary ceasefire in Oleshky and its potential impact on U.S. President Donald Trump’s planned trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine and the United States.

According to Ambassador Taylor, the situation in Oleshky was horrific, and many people around the world, particularly Ukrainians, have been making the case that this horrible humanitarian situation needs to be addressed.

The city has been under constant shelling, and the residents who remain there have been left without drinking water or food. The routes out of the city have been mined.

Eventually, Taylor said, high profile figures such as Pope Leo XIV, the White House and Melania Trump took notice: "They raised it to a higher level of attention, and put some pressure on Putin." On October 23, an agreement on a temporary, localized ceasefire around the city was announced.

While it is impossible to say for sure, he believed it forced Putin to agree to a ceasefire: "It looked so bad for the Russians that they had to act."

The ceasefire was initially scheduled to start on October 29, but it went into effect earlier, on October 27, and is expected to remain in place through November 1.

Regarding U.S. involvement, Taylor described the ceasefire agreement as long overdue: "This should have happened a long time ago. The delay only prolonged the suffering of Ukrainians living in Russian-controlled territories."

According to Taylor, it is yet unknown whether this localized ceasefire could affect the upcoming scheduled trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and U.S., either at the technical level or at the summit level. The experience with prisoner exchanges and the P.O.W. exchanges between Russian and Ukraine demonstrate that progress can be achieved: "It shows that it's possible for the Ukrainians and the Russians to have an agreement, having a talk come to some understanding about how things can work. And that may be a good signal."

Taylor pointed that the Ukrainians have made it very clear that they're willing to talk and have already made some compromises, for example, about freezing the front lines.

"Many people, many Ukrainians want to push the Russians all the way out of their country back to 1991 borders. So, the point is, the Ukrainians have already made compromises. The Ukrainians have already proposed ceasefires. The Ukrainians have agreed with Trump on an energy cease fire."

The single obstacle for a successful trilateral meeting is the president of Russia: "There's one obstacle. There's just one obstacle, and that's Vladimir Putin," said Taylor.

articles.title: UN reports sharp increase in opium poppy cultivation and production in Afghanistan
articles.body:
Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

Opium poppy cultivation in Afghanistan increased by 330 percent and opium production rose by 400 percent in 2026 compared to last year, according to a new survey by the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime.

The survey released Thursday found that opium poppy cultivation increased from 10,000 hectares in 2025 to 43,000 in 2026, while estimated opium production rose from 300 tons in 2025 to just under 1,500 tons in 2026.

The Taliban’s Ministry of Interior rejected the report, saying that its findings contradict official figures.

Before the Taliban’s takeover in 2021, Afghanistan was one of the world’s largest opiate suppliers. The group, however, outlawed the cultivation of narcotics nationwide in April 2022, which led to a massive decline in opium poppy production.

The UNODC report said that despite the sharp increase in 2026, opium poppy cultivation remained below the pre-ban levels, when more than 200,000 hectares of land were planted with poppy.

The report said the Taliban government reported eradicating about 22,000 hectares of poppy fields in 2026. UNODC, however, said that it could not independently verify the figures.

UNODC said that Afghan farmers have found ways to get around the Taliban’s restrictions.

The report said that opium poppy cultivation expanded from 29 provinces in 2025 to 34 provinces, and that only the southern Zabul province was opium free.

“The farmers are concealing small poppy plots within cereal fields or inside walled compounds or are planting and harvesting at staggered intervals to reduce the risk of detection,” said the report.

UNODC also reported that the prices of opium fell from $570 to $500 per kilogram compared with the previous year. However, prices remained three times higher than the seasonal averages before the Taliban’s ban on poppy cultivation.

A Kabul-based agricultural expert, who requested anonymity, told VOA that the survey paints a grim picture of unemployment in Afghanistan.

“It shows how people are struggling to cope with economic consequences of the Taliban’s rule,” he said.

The expert also said that the report calls into question the Taliban’s claim of having complete control over the country.

“The Taliban, because of that, say that they have reduced poppy cultivation to zero,” he added.

On Tuesday, Taliban Foreign Minister Amir Khan Muttaqi said group's fight against narcotics was one of the its greatest achievements.

The expert, however, said the new report “damages the Taliban’s global image’ on the issue.
